Quality of hire is a composite metric that measures how much value a new employee adds to your organization after they start. It combines job performance, retention, hiring manager satisfaction, and time-to-productivity into a single score - and right now, most recruiting teams can't measure it. According to [SHRM's 2025 recruiting benchmarking release](https://www.shrm.org/mena/about/press-room/shrm-releases-2025-benchmarking-reports--how-does-your-organizat), only about 20% of organizations track quality of hire at all.

Starker still is the ambition-execution gap when you look at the numbers. A 2024 study by [Aptitude Research and Crosschq](https://info.crosschq.com/hubfs/Downloads/Crosschq-Aptitude-Research-Report-Quality-of-Hire.pdf) found that 75% of HR and talent acquisition leaders name this metric one of their leading priorities. Yet only 38% of companies consistently deliver high-quality hires, and even among those effective organizations, just 23% measure it comprehensively. Most organizations know hiring quality matters. Very few have built the [infrastructure to track it](/blog/recruitment-analytics-tools/).

That's a problem worth solving. LinkedIn's Future of Recruiting 2025 report found that 89% of talent acquisition professionals agree tracking hiring outcomes this way will become increasingly important - yet only 25% feel highly confident their organization can actually do it. There's a 64-point gap between knowing this metric matters and being able to act on it.

This guide gives you the formula, the scorecard, and the step-by-step process to close that gap. You'll learn which metrics to track, how to weight them, and how AI sourcing tools are helping teams improve quality of hire before candidates even enter the [recruitment funnel](https://www.pin.com/blog/recruitment-funnel-benchmarks/).

> **TL;DR:**
>
> - **The formula is a weighted composite.** QoH = (job performance + retention + hiring manager satisfaction + cultural fit) / number of indicators. A weighted scorecard beats the simple average for most teams.
> - **The measurement gap is enormous.** 75% of HR and TA leaders call quality of hire a leading priority, yet only 38% of companies consistently deliver quality hires ([Aptitude Research/Crosschq, 2024](https://info.crosschq.com/hubfs/Downloads/Crosschq-Aptitude-Research-Report-Quality-of-Hire.pdf)), and just 20% of organizations track it at all ([SHRM, 2025](https://www.shrm.org/mena/about/press-room/shrm-releases-2025-benchmarking-reports--how-does-your-organizat)).
> - **Bad hires are expensive.** Employers report losing an average of $14,900 per bad hire ([CareerBuilder/Harris Poll](https://www.hrdive.com/news/careerbuilder-74-of-employers-admit-hiring-the-wrong-candidate/512577/)), while [McKinsey](https://www.mckinsey.com/capabilities/people-and-organizational-performance/our-insights/increasing-your-return-on-talent-the-moves-and-metrics-that-matter) finds top performers in highly critical roles deliver 800% more productivity than average performers.
> - **Track performance and retention first.** 66% of TA teams track job performance and 60% track retention; time-to-productivity (26%) is underrated and highly actionable through better onboarding.
> - **Improve it upstream, not downstream.** AI sourcing tools that surface better-matched candidates raise quality of hire before anyone enters the pipeline.

## Why Quality of Hire Is Recruiting's Most Important Metric

Top performers in highly critical roles deliver 800% more productivity than average performers in the same role, which makes hiring quality the only recruiting metric with a direct line to business output. When you look at the cost of getting it wrong, the urgency makes sense.

In a [Harris Poll survey for CareerBuilder](https://www.hrdive.com/news/careerbuilder-74-of-employers-admit-hiring-the-wrong-candidate/512577/), 74% of U.S. employers admitted hiring the wrong person in the prior year, at an average cost of $14,900 per bad hire. Treat that self-reported 2017 figure as a floor. It doesn't include the productivity hit to the team that has to absorb the workload while you start the search over.

Getting it right carries an equally dramatic upside. [McKinsey research](https://www.mckinsey.com/capabilities/people-and-organizational-performance/our-insights/increasing-your-return-on-talent-the-moves-and-metrics-that-matter) shows that top performers in highly critical roles deliver 800% more productivity than average performers in the same role. The difference between a quality hire and an average one isn't marginal. It's a multiplier that compounds across every project, quarter, and year that person stays.

Individual roles are only part of the picture. Research from the [Josh Bersin Company's Systemic HR study](https://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/josh-bersin-company-systemic-hr-model-emerges-as-global-2025-hr-best-practice-302390014.html) found that organizations running an integrated, data-driven HR model are 2x more likely to exceed their financial targets. They're also 12x more likely to reach high levels of workforce productivity. Measuring hire quality isn't just a recruiting improvement; it's a business outcome lever.

Yet most recruiting teams still measure success by speed and volume. Time-to-fill gets tracked obsessively. Cost-per-hire gets reported to leadership every quarter. But quality of hire - the metric that tells you whether your recruiting process is actually working - often gets left on the whiteboard as a "nice to have."

Think about what happens when you optimize for speed without measuring quality. You fill a role in 25 days, celebrate the efficiency, and three months later the hire is underperforming or already looking for their next job. [SHRM's benchmarking data](https://www.shrm.org/topics-tools/research/2025-recruiting-benchmarking) puts the median time-to-fill for nonexecutive roles at 39 days. Cutting that to 25 days means nothing if the person you hired doesn't work out and you're back at day zero within a quarter.

That's changing fast. The shift from efficiency metrics to outcome metrics is accelerating across recruiting. Teams that don't adapt will keep optimizing for speed while losing on the metric that actually matters to the business. Building a proper [HR analytics practice](https://www.pin.com/blog/talent-analytics-guide/) gives TA leaders the infrastructure to track it alongside other workforce metrics in a single framework.

## What Goes Into a Quality of Hire Score?

A quality of hire score (sometimes called a quality of hire index) is a composite of 4-5 post-hire indicators measured over time, not a single quality of hire metric you pull from your ATS. According to LinkedIn's 2025 data on how TA teams approach this metric, here's how professionals currently break down quality of hire measurement:

<figure style="margin:2rem 0;padding:0;line-height:0"><img src="data:image/svg+xml;base64," alt="How TA Teams Measure Quality of Hire" style="width:100%;height:auto;display:block;border-radius:12px"></figure>

Two things stand out. First, job performance (66%) and retention (60%) dominate as the most tracked indicators by a wide margin. Everything else sits below 45%. Second, time-to-productivity - one of the most actionable metrics in the entire list - didn't even crack the top eight. Only 26% of teams track it, according to the same LinkedIn data. That's a missed opportunity, because ramp time is something you can directly influence through [better onboarding](/blog/ai-onboarding-tools/) and stronger [12-month retention](/blog/skills-vs-degree-hiring-study/) outcomes at the sourcing stage.

The standard quality of hire formula averages these indicators into a single percentage score:

**QoH = (Indicator 1 + Indicator 2 + Indicator 3 + ... Indicator N) / N**

For example, if you track four indicators and a new hire scores 85% on performance, 90% on retention, 75% on manager satisfaction, and 80% on cultural fit:

**QoH = (85 + 90 + 75 + 80) / 4 = 82.5%**

But this basic formula has a flaw: it treats every indicator equally. A hire who performs brilliantly but quits after three months gets the same retention credit as one who stays five years. A candidate who fits the culture perfectly but takes 9 months to reach full productivity scores the same as someone who ships work in week two.

Most experienced TA teams address this limitation with a weighted model that prioritizes the indicators that matter most for the role and the organization.

## How to Build a Weighted Quality of Hire Scorecard

A weighted quality of hire scorecard produces more accurate scores because it reflects what actually matters for each role and your organization's priorities. This commonly used quality of hire model works as a starting point for most recruiting functions:

| Indicator | Weight | What It Measures | When to Assess |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Job Performance | 40% | Manager ratings, goal completion, output quality | 90-day and annual review |
| Retention | 20% | Whether the hire stays past 12 months | 12-month mark |
| Time-to-Productivity | 20% | How quickly the hire reaches full output | 30/60/90-day check-ins |
| Cultural Fit | 10% | Peer feedback, team integration scores | 90-day survey |
| Manager Satisfaction | 10% | Hiring manager's overall rating of the hire | 90-day and 6-month check-in |

With this weighting, a hire who performs well but takes 6 months to ramp up scores differently than one who hits the ground running but leaves after 8 months. That distinction matters when you're trying to improve your sourcing strategy based on real outcomes.

<figure style="margin:2rem 0;padding:0;line-height:0"><img src="data:image/svg+xml;base64," alt="A Starting Weighted Quality of Hire Model" style="width:100%;height:auto;display:block;border-radius:12px"></figure>

To calculate quality of hire with these weights, plug each indicator score into the weighted formula:

**Weighted QoH = (Performance x 0.40) + (Retention x 0.20) + (Time-to-Productivity x 0.20) + (Cultural Fit x 0.10) + (Manager Satisfaction x 0.10)**

Example: A software engineer scores 90% on performance, 100% on retention (still employed at 12 months), 70% on time-to-productivity (took longer than expected to ramp), 85% on cultural fit, and 80% on manager satisfaction.

**Weighted QoH = (90 x 0.40) + (100 x 0.20) + (70 x 0.20) + (85 x 0.10) + (80 x 0.10) = 36 + 20 + 14 + 8.5 + 8 = 86.5%**

An 86.5% score signals a strong hire. Most organizations consider anything above 80% a quality hire, 60-80% average, and below 60% a poor hire. But those thresholds should be calibrated to your own data over time - what counts as "quality" for an enterprise sales role might look different than a junior marketing coordinator.

Adjust the weights based on role type. For customer-facing roles, bump cultural fit to 20% and reduce time-to-productivity to 10%. For technical roles where output is measurable, performance might deserve 50% weight. The key is making the weights intentional rather than treating every indicator as equally important.

### When to Measure Each Indicator

QoH isn't a one-time calculation. It unfolds over a timeline, and the data you collect at each stage tells a different part of the story:

-   **Pre-hire (before day 1):** Source quality, interview scores, [skills assessment](/blog/skills-assessment-guide/) results. These are leading indicators that predict post-hire outcomes before that data exists.
-   **Days 1-30:** Onboarding completion rate, early cultural fit signals, new hire satisfaction survey.
-   **Days 31-90:** First performance check-in, hiring manager satisfaction survey, time-to-productivity milestones.
-   **Months 3-6:** Skills match verification, peer and team feedback, productivity benchmarks against role expectations.
-   **Months 6-12:** Formal performance review score, retention status, promotion eligibility assessment.

Most recruiting functions run their first quality of hire calculation at the 90-day mark. The 12-month mark is where the full picture comes together, because retention - one of the highest-weighted indicators - only becomes meaningful after a full year. Recent data from [Employ Inc.'s 2026 research](https://www.globenewswire.com/news-release/2026/03/02/3247298/0/en/The-Great-Stay-Continues-Employ-Inc-Research-Finds-49-Percent-Decrease-in-First-Year-Turnover.html) shows first-year turnover across its customers fell from 23.7% in 2024 to 12.1% in 2025. Employ ties that drop to a low-quit labor market, not better hiring. Career histories tell a longer story. Based on Pin's data, in a sample of 720,000+ US job starts from 2022 to mid-2024, 26.3% of roles ended within 12 months and 12.7% ended within six. Roughly one in four new hires leaving inside a year is why 12-month retention earns its weight in every quality of hire scorecard. A calm market can hide weak matches for a while, but that retention check eventually surfaces them.

## Why Do Most TA Teams Struggle to Measure Quality of Hire?

QoH measurement fails because it requires connecting data across systems that rarely talk to each other: ATS source attribution, HRIS retention records, performance management scores, and hiring manager satisfaction surveys. The answer shows up clearly in LinkedIn's 2025 data. There's a massive gap between how important TA leaders think this metric is and how confident they feel measuring it.

<figure style="margin:2rem 0;padding:0;line-height:0"><img src="data:image/svg+xml;base64," alt="The Quality of Hire Confidence Gap" style="width:100%;height:auto;display:block;border-radius:12px"></figure>

That 64-percentage-point gap between importance and confidence isn't a knowledge problem. It's a data infrastructure problem. This metric requires connecting information across systems that usually don't talk to each other:

-   **Your ATS** holds candidate source data and hiring process information
-   **Your HRIS** holds retention and compensation data
-   **Your performance management tool** holds review scores and goal attainment
-   **Your hiring managers** hold subjective satisfaction assessments that live in spreadsheets or nowhere at all

Pulling these data points into [a single composite score](/blog/hiring-health-index/) means either manual spreadsheet work that doesn't scale, or integrated platforms that connect recruiting evidence to post-hire outcomes. Most organizations haven't invested in that connection.

There's also the subjectivity problem. "Manager satisfaction" and "cultural fit" mean different things to different managers. Without standardized rubrics - where a score of 8 means the same thing whether it comes from the engineering director or the sales VP - these indicators vary wildly across teams and don't produce useful benchmarks.

And then there's the time lag. You won't know if a hire was truly "quality" until 6-12 months after they start. By then, the recruiter has moved on to other requisitions. The feedback loop between "where did this candidate come from?" and "how are they performing?" breaks. Without that connection, you can't tell whether your sourcing strategy is actually producing quality hires or just filling seats.

The good news: you don't need to solve all of these problems at once. Start with the indicators you already have access to, standardize how you score them, and build the feedback loop incrementally. Even a simple post-hire measurement system is dramatically better than none. Recruiting functions that start tracking - even imperfectly - gain a compounding advantage over those still flying blind on their most important outcome.

### Which ATS Platforms Measure Quality of Hire?

No ATS measures quality of hire end to end on its own, because the post-hire half of the score lives in your HRIS and performance management tool. What an applicant tracking system can expose natively are the upstream signals: source attribution (which channel produced this hire), time-to-fill by source, and offer acceptance rate by requisition. Each of those is a useful pre-hire quality of hire KPI, and they're the best quality of hire metrics to pull from any ATS. The gap is the join. Teams that use their ATS well export source data and match it to 90-day performance scores and 12-month retention, even in a spreadsheet, to finish the calculation. A dedicated quality of hire tool or people-analytics layer only pays off once that join exists, so build the manual version first and buy software when the spreadsheet stops scaling.

## Candidate Fraud: A Growing Threat to Hire Quality

There's a variable threatening quality of hire that barely existed five years ago: candidate fraud. [Gartner predicts that 1 in 4 candidate profiles worldwide will be fake by 2028](https://www.gartner.com/en/newsroom/press-releases/2025-07-31-gartner-survey-shows-just-26-percent-of-job-applicants-trust-ai-will-fairly-evaluate-them). In the same 2025 survey of roughly 3,000 job candidates, 6% admitted to interview fraud, such as having someone else stand in for them or using AI to feed them answers.

This isn't hypothetical. It's happening now, and it directly undermines hire quality. If a candidate misrepresents their skills or uses generative AI to pass assessments they couldn't handle independently, your performance scores, retention rates, and time-to-productivity all take a hit once they're on the job.

How do you protect quality of hire from fraud?

-   **Skills assessments with proctoring.** [Gartner](https://www.gartner.com/en/newsroom/press-releases/2025-10-07-gartner-says-ai-revolution-and-cost-pressures-are-two-forces-driving-the-top-four-trends-for-talent-acquisition-in-2026) predicts that by 2027, 75% of hiring processes will include certifications and tests for workplace AI proficiency. Verified assessments filter out candidates who can't back up their resumes.
-   **Multi-signal verification.** Don't rely on a single data point. Cross-reference interview performance with assessment scores, [reference checks](/blog/reference-check-best-practices/), and work samples.
-   **Verified candidate databases.** Sourcing platforms that maintain hundreds of millions of verified profiles - rather than relying on self-reported or scraped data - reduce the odds of fake candidates entering your funnel.
-   **Structured interviews.** Standardized questions with scoring rubrics make it harder for candidates to game the process and easier for hiring managers to evaluate consistently.

Fraud risk reinforces why top-of-funnel quality matters. If your sourcing pulls from verified, multi-source databases rather than user-submitted profiles, fewer fraudulent candidates make it to the interview stage in the first place. And when your sourcing tool matches on verified skills and experience patterns - not just what someone claims on a resume - the signal-to-noise ratio improves before a hiring manager ever sees a profile.

## How to Measure Quality of Hire in 5 Steps

To measure quality of hire, pick three indicators you already have access to, standardize how you score them, and run your first calculation at the 90-day mark. No integrated systems or new software are required. LinkedIn's 2025 data shows 93% of TA professionals believe accurately assessing candidate skills is crucial for improving quality of hire - and this process gives you the structure to act on that insight. Here's a practical approach that works even if your tools aren't fully integrated yet.

### Step 1: Pick 3-4 Indicators

Don't try to track everything. Start with the indicators you already have data for. Most teams can access job performance ratings, retention data, and hiring manager satisfaction without buying new software. Add one "stretch" indicator - like time-to-productivity - to push your measurement forward. Three solid indicators with clean data will give you a more reliable score than eight indicators measured inconsistently. Only about 20% of organizations currently track this metric at all, according to [SHRM's 2025 benchmarking release](https://www.shrm.org/mena/about/press-room/shrm-releases-2025-benchmarking-reports--how-does-your-organizat) - which means even a basic three-indicator system puts your team ahead of most.

### Step 2: Define Your Scoring Scale

Standardize how you score each indicator. A 1-10 scale works well for most teams. The critical part: define what each score means in writing. "Exceeds all performance goals within the first 90 days" is a 9 or 10. "Meets most expectations but needs coaching on two key competencies" is a 6 or 7. Without written definitions, managers score based on gut feel, and your data becomes noise. Share the rubric with every hiring manager before they submit scores so everyone is working from the same baseline.

### Step 3: Set Your Weights

Use the weighting model from the scorecard section above as a starting point: performance 40%, retention 20%, time-to-productivity 20%, cultural fit 10%, manager satisfaction 10%. Then adjust based on what your leadership team cares about most. If retention is your biggest problem, increase its weight. If your team ships product and speed-to-contribution matters most, bump time-to-productivity.

### Step 4: Calculate at 90 Days and 12 Months

Run your first score at the 90-day mark using whatever data is available. Run the full calculation at 12 months when retention data becomes meaningful. Compare scores across recruiters, sourcing channels, and departments to find patterns. Which sources produce the highest-quality hires? Which teams have the biggest gap between interview scores and actual performance? These patterns are where the real insight lives.

### Step 5: Connect Quality Back to Sourcing

This is where the real value sits. Once you have post-hire scores, trace it back to where each candidate came from. Are hires from employee referrals outperforming those from job boards? Are candidates sourced through AI platforms showing better [time-to-hire](https://www.pin.com/blog/time-to-hire-metrics-ai/) and retention? This feedback loop turns QoH from a reporting metric into a [recruiting ROI](https://www.pin.com/blog/recruiting-roi-ai-tools/) tool that improves your sourcing strategy over time.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### What is quality of hire and how do you measure it?

Quality of hire is a composite metric that measures how much value a new employee adds after starting. You calculate it by averaging post-hire indicators - typically job performance, retention, hiring manager satisfaction, and cultural fit - on a percentage scale. According to [SHRM's 2025 benchmarking release](https://www.shrm.org/mena/about/press-room/shrm-releases-2025-benchmarking-reports--how-does-your-organizat), only about 20% of organizations track quality of hire at all.

### What are the 5 C's of hiring?

The 5 C's of hiring are a candidate evaluation framework that goes beyond technical credentials:

1. **Character** - integrity and trustworthiness
2. **Competency** - skills, experience, and the ability to do the job
3. **Chemistry** - how well the candidate fits the existing team's working style
4. **Culture** - values alignment with the organization's mission
5. **Calling or Contribution** - motivation and the unique value the candidate brings

Applied alongside quality of hire measurement, the 5 C's help recruiters standardize assessments before the hire - so post-hire scores on retention and performance are more predictable.

### What is a good quality of hire score?

Most organizations consider a score above 80% (on a 100-point scale) a quality hire, 60-80% average, and below 60% a poor hire. The exact threshold depends on your industry, role complexity, and which indicators you weight most heavily. Track your scores over time to build internal benchmarks rather than relying solely on universal cutoffs. Your own trend data will be more useful than any industry average.

### How does AI improve quality of hire in recruiting?

AI improves quality of hire primarily at the top of funnel by matching candidates to roles based on skills and experience patterns rather than keywords alone. LinkedIn's 2025 research found that companies running the most skills-based searches are 12% more likely to make a quality hire. AI-enabled companies also hire 2-3x faster, per Josh Bersin Company research with AMS.

### What metrics should recruiters track for quality of hire?

Job performance (66% of TA teams), retention and turnover (60%), hiring manager satisfaction (44%), and skills match (44%) are the most commonly tracked indicators, according to LinkedIn's 2025 data. Start with these four and add time-to-productivity once you have the infrastructure to measure it consistently. Use a weighted formula to reflect which indicators matter most for each role type.

### How much does a bad hire cost?

Employers in a Harris Poll survey for CareerBuilder reported losing an average of $14,900 per bad hire, and 74% admitted hiring the wrong person in the prior year. For context, [SHRM's 2025 benchmarking release](https://www.shrm.org/mena/about/press-room/shrm-releases-2025-benchmarking-reports--how-does-your-organizat) puts the average cost-per-hire alone at $5,475 for nonexecutive roles and $35,879 for executive positions. That's before counting productivity losses, team disruption, and the cost of restarting the search.

## Start Measuring What Matters

Quality of hire is the metric that separates recruiting teams who fill seats from teams who build organizations. The formula isn't complicated - it's getting the right data, weighting it properly, and connecting post-hire outcomes back to sourcing decisions so you can improve over time.

Every percentage point gain in hiring quality compounds across your organization. Better hires perform better, stay longer, ramp faster, and contribute to teams that attract other high performers. The ROI of measuring and improving it dwarfs the return on shaving a few days off time-to-fill. When McKinsey finds top performers in highly critical roles deliver 800% more productivity than average ones, even a modest improvement in sourcing accuracy pays for itself quickly.

Closing the 64-point confidence gap between importance (89%) and measurement capability (25%) requires a starting point, not a perfect system. Organizations that begin now - even with three indicators and a spreadsheet - will build the feedback loop that turns recruiting from a cost center into a competitive advantage.

Start with three indicators. Calculate your first score at 90 days. Trace it back to your sourcing channels. The patterns will tell you where to invest - and where to stop wasting budget.
